clue.text: Blue magazine from US for when there's no work doable

definitions.note: a clause describing a period, standing for the noun

parts.note: feeling blue is feeling down
Time is a well-known American news magazine

explanation.surface: A gloomy American magazine is only fit to be read when there is nothing else to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' looks like a colour of the magazine's cover, but it is a mood word.
explanation.definitionFit: Downtime is the period when machines or staff are idle and no productive work can be carried out.

clue.text: Stone to fail to gather moss — even at this pace?

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight of fourteen pounds
the proverb says a rolling stone gathers no moss, so rolling is what makes moss fail to gather

explanation.surface: The proverbial rolling stone gathers no moss: would that still hold if it moved slowly?
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a rolling stone gathers no moss' supplies the second piece; the question mark admits the whimsy of a stone ambling along.
explanation.definitionFit: A stroll is a leisurely walking speed, so it names a slow, unhurried gait or tempo of movement.

clue.text: Extremely anxious Pastor hurried over, brought in help

parts.note: P is a dictionary abbreviation for pastor

indicators.note: something brought in is taken inside, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: aid is help
to hurry is to run, past tense ran
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A nervous clergyman dashed across and called in assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: The running and the over go inside the help, after the clergyman's single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Paranoid in everyday use describes someone excessively worried or suspicious, far beyond ordinary nervousness.

clue.text: Sheep initially led away from Sussex town

indicators.note: being taken away from something means removal, so letters drop out

parts.note: Lewes is the county town of East Sussex in southern England

indicators.note: initially points to the very first letter of the word it sits with

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A flock is being driven out of a market town in Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewes is the county town of East Sussex; lose its first L and the plural sheep remain.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewes are female sheep, and the plural form matches the clue word, which can also be plural.

clue.text: Wait to follow soprano with lots of celebrities

parts.note: S is the musical abbreviation for soprano
to tarry is to linger or wait

explanation.surface: Someone waits behind an opera singer surrounded by famous people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To follow' places the waiting word after the singer's single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A starry cast or line-up is one full of famous performers, star being a common word for a celebrity.

clue.text: Turned up source of cod roe eaten by couple in a flash?

definitions.note: a phrase describing speed, standing for the adjective

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning something up means it now reads bottom to top
the source of something is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: first letter of the fish

indicators.note: whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: a romantic couple is called an item
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone appears suddenly with the source of some cod roe that a pair devoured in moments.
explanation.walkthrough: Fish eggs go inside the couple, the fish's first letter goes in front, and the whole string reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A meteoric rise is astonishingly rapid, like a shooting star streaking briefly across the sky.

clue.text: Description of classic children's stories is exactly right

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the title word of Rudyard Kipling's 1902 collection of animal origin tales
second meaning: arranged precisely as it should be

explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's 1902 collection, including how the elephant got its trunk, is called Just So Stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase labels Kipling's famous collection and also means neat, precise and perfectly arranged.

clue.text: Shakespearean legal expert left one amazed at the outset

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare lawyer departed, leaving someone astonished from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as a verb of departing; here it is the nautical side.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Merchant of Venice Portia disguises herself as a young lawyer and wins Antonio's case in court.

clue.text: A measure of power depicted by the water of the French painter

parts.note: the watt is the unit of power
eau is French for water

explanation.surface: Someone depicts the force of water in a French painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depicted by' sounds like the painter's business, but it only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Antoine Watteau was an eighteenth-century French artist famous for his fêtes galantes, so he is a painter.

clue.text: Very taken by entirely overlooking duplication

indicators.note: to overlook a duplication is to ignore the repeated part, so the second copy is dropped

parts.note: in toto is Latin for entirely, as a whole

explanation.surface: Someone besotted manages to ignore all the repetition.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase for 'entirely' ends with a doubled TO; ignore one of the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: To be into something or someone is informal for being keen on or enthusiastic about them.

clue.text: Not here, circling planet, taking everything in?

indicators.note: to circle something is to go right round it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: someone not here is absent
an orb is a sphere, a poetic word for a planet

explanation.surface: A satellite, away from home and orbiting a planet, observes everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition: 'taking everything in' usually means noticing, but here it is soaking up liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something absorbent soaks up liquid, so it literally takes in whatever it touches, like a sponge or towel.

clue.text: Uncountable numbers backing Elizabeth to lead rugby team

indicators.note: going backwards means reading from right to left

parts.note: Liz is a short form of Elizabeth
the British and Irish Lions are a touring rugby union side

explanation.surface: Huge crowds are supporting Elizabeth as she captains a rugby side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like supporting, but it turns the short name round; 'to lead' puts it in front of the team.
explanation.definitionFit: Zillions is informal for an enormous, unspecified quantity, too many to be counted precisely.

clue.text: Underhand, dodgy character promoting energy

indicators.note: to promote is to move up, so a letter is shifted to an earlier place in the word

parts.note: a snake is a treacherous, untrustworthy person
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A shady character is pushing some energy product.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the E near the end of the untrustworthy creature and move it up two places, in this down entry nearer the top.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective sneak means done stealthily or by surprise, as in a sneak attack, which is underhand.

clue.text: Concern about a regressive plant

indicators.note: regressive means going backwards, so the letters run in the other direction
about means around, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: a worry is a concern
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone frets over a plant that seems to be going backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regressive' governs the whole of the concern with the article inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarrow is a common flowering herb of meadows and verges, Achillea millefolium, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Philosopher recalled core of puzzle? Not half!

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters come back in the reverse direction

parts.note: the middle of the word puzzle is a double Z; not both halves of that pair leaves one of them, written out in full

explanation.surface: A thinker remembers the heart of a puzzle, with an emphatic exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is a British exclamation meaning 'very much', but here it asks for half of the double Z in the middle of puzzle, read as the phrase ONE Z.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeno of Elea was an ancient Greek thinker known for his paradoxes about motion, such as Achilles and the tortoise.

clue.text: Love bold cheers around English work by Gilbert and Sullivan?

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: pert means cheeky or bold
E is the abbreviation for English
ta is British slang for thanks, as is cheers

explanation.surface: Fans loudly cheer an English comic opera by the Victorian duo.
explanation.walkthrough: The bold word wraps the English letter, with love before and cheers after. 'Cheers' and 'ta' are both British for 'thanks'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert and Sullivan wrote light comic operas such as The Mikado, an example of the operetta form, hence the question mark.

clue.text: US nerd, dumb, heartless, taking the piss?

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another
without a heart means the middle of the word is removed

parts.note: taken as written
piss is vulgar slang for urine, as is wee

explanation.surface: An American geek is called stupid and cruelly mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking the piss' is British slang for mocking someone; here it literally means taking in some urine.
explanation.definitionFit: Dweeb is American slang for a boring, socially awkward or studious person, essentially a nerd.

clue.text: Drunken bird is enthralling in drinking song

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece is held inside another
a drunk staggers about unsteadily, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tipsy woman is captivating everyone with a song in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is British slang for a young woman, which sharpens the pub picture; the word is used only as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A brindisi is a song sung while raising a toast, as in the famous drinking chorus in Verdi's La traviata.

clue.text: Copper following, bringing restraint

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
ff is the abbreviation for 'and following' pages or lines

explanation.surface: A police officer in pursuit brings handcuffs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is British slang for a police officer, but here it is the metal; ff, as in 'pp. 10ff', abbreviates 'and following'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuff, short for handcuff, is a metal ring locked round the wrist to restrain a prisoner.

clue.text: Rather like meal's splendour

parts.note: meal is coarsely ground grain, a kind of flour
the suffix -ish means somewhat, rather like

explanation.surface: A dinner that is fairly grand might be called splendid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meal' suggests dinner but means ground grain; the suffix '-ish' attaches after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A flourish is an ostentatious, showy display or embellishment, which carries a sense of grandeur and magnificence.

clue.text: Lots of people initially ignored special measure

indicators.note: ignoring what comes first means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: the masses are large numbers of people
S is an abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: Many people were overlooked from the start when a special measure was introduced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special measure' looks like one phrase, but 'special' belongs to the wordplay and 'measure' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess is to evaluate or gauge the size, value or quality of something, which is to measure it.

clue.text: Magnificent bird released from US sporting event

indicators.note: whatever is released from something leaves it, so those letters drop out

parts.note: the Super Bowl is the championship game of American football
an owl is a bird

explanation.surface: A splendid bird is set free at a big American sports fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the nocturnal bird from the end of the American football final.
explanation.definitionFit: Superb is an adjective meaning excellent or splendid, the same sense as magnificent.

clue.text: Fish with fins sailor placed in chair

indicators.note: something placed in another thing sits inside it

parts.note: a chair is a seat
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a standard abbreviation for a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor is placed in a chair with a fish for company.
explanation.walkthrough: The sailor goes inside the chair, splitting it after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea bat is a name for the batfish, known for broad wing-like fins that resemble a bat's wings.

clue.text: Storage for blades US fort deployed around start of month

indicators.note: troops deployed around something are spread out to surround it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: Fort Knox in Kentucky holds the US gold reserve
1 Feb, written I FEB with the Roman numeral, is the first day of a month

explanation.surface: Blades are stored at an American fort, with troops deployed at the start of a month.
explanation.walkthrough: Fort Knox is the famous US army base and gold depository; the first of February, as Roman I plus the abbreviation FEB, sits inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A knife box is a container, often with compartments, for keeping cutlery or knives, which have blades.

clue.text: Kinky sex with duo? A large number leaving

indicators.note: kinky means twisted or bent, so the letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pair's adventurous bedroom habits drive lots of people to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' just joins the two words of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An exodus is a mass departure of people, named after the Israelites' flight from Egypt.

clue.text: Quiet minister felt bad but took control

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet
Rev, reverend, is the title of a minister of religion
to ail is to feel unwell

explanation.surface: A softly spoken clergyman felt unwell but took charge anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But' simply joins the wordplay to the definition, while making the surface a story of triumph over illness.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to win out or gain the upper hand, so prevailed means gained mastery or dominance.

clue.text: Fine to follow story willingly (though less so these days)

parts.note: a story is an untruth, a lie
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads

explanation.surface: Someone is happy to go along with a tale, though fewer people are nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is part of the definition: it says the answer is archaic, a pun on 'less willingly' too.
explanation.definitionFit: Lief is an old-fashioned word for gladly, as in 'I would as lief stay', now rarely used.

clue.text: Former King stabbing Old English monster

indicators.note: a blade that stabs goes into something, so one piece is pushed inside another

parts.note: OE is the abbreviation for Old English
GR, Georgius Rex, is the cipher of a past King George

explanation.surface: An ancient English ruler slays a monster, like a scene from an old epic.
explanation.walkthrough: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George, seen on old postboxes; it goes inside the abbreviation for the early language.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating giant of folklore, a frightening monster in fairy tales.

clue.text: Speed round reversing vehicle in competitive situation

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: rate is speed

indicators.note: something reversing goes backwards, so its letters run the other way

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A fast lap with a car going backwards, in the middle of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversing vehicle' looks like a car backing up, which it is: the vehicle's letters run backwards inside the speed word.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the fierce, exhausting struggle for success in modern working life.

clue.text: Put down fruit drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to suppress or crush, as with a rebellion
second meaning: a concentrated fruit cordial diluted with water

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a squash is a sweet fruit concentrate topped up with water.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to crush or suppress, and the British noun names a diluted fruit cordial.
